The patent argument is more complicated than it looks. Semaglutide is a modified peptide, and Novo Nordisk built one of the most valuable pharmaceutical franchises in history around it. The patent barrier isn't what's keeping BPC-157 or CJC-1295 out of mainstream medicine.

What's actually keeping them out is that the compounding pharmacy route they currently travel, operating under FDA 503A and 503B frameworks, is structurally fragile. It's not a long-term home. The FDA has been tightening compounding rules steadily, and there's no middle ground that survives that pressure indefinitely. Compounds that don't enter formal pharmaceutical development pipelines don't get preserved in amber, they get excluded.

The safety and efficacy question is real but it's almost secondary to the regulatory mechanics. A peptide can have a compelling biological rationale and genuine clinical interest from physicians and it still faces a binary outcome: someone funds the trials and the IND process, or it gets squeezed out of the compounding channel with nowhere else to go.

The same filtration logic applies to the broader integrative medicine space. What survives the transition to mainstream care isn't what wins scientific arguments. It's what gets a CPT code, a reimbursement pathway, and measurement tools that satisfy payer requirements. Everything else stays in the cash-pay economy regardless of clinical merit.
